claim: Branched microtubule networks preferentially nucleate new branches near the minus-ends of pre-existing microtubules.
source: Surprisingly, new branched MTs preferentially originate near the minus-ends of pre-existing MTs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations described in the abstract and demonstrated through spatial profile measurements in Figure 1A and Figure 2A-B.

claim: A sequential reaction model consisting of deposition of nucleation sites followed by rate-limiting nucleation of branches reproduces the measured spatial profile of nucleation.
source: A sequential reaction model, consisting of deposition of nucleation sites on an existing MT, followed by rate-limiting nucleation of branches, reproduces the measured spatial profile of nucleation, the distribution of MT plus-ends and tubulin intensity.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling and comparison with experimental data shown in Figures 1D, 2A-E.

claim: TPX2 is deposited on pre-existing microtubules before augmin/γ-TuRC binding results in nucleation of branched microtubules.
source: By regulating the availability of the branching effectors TPX2, augmin and γ-TuRC, combined with single-molecule observations, we show that first TPX2 is deposited on pre-existing MTs, followed by binding of augmin/γ-TuRC to result in the nucleation of branched MTs.
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments (Figure 4A-C) and direct visualization of TPX2 binding (Figure 4D-E).

claim: The mitotic spindle is responsible for segregating chromosomes during cell division.
source: The mitotic spindle is a complex and dynamic macromolecular machine that is responsible for segregating chromosomes during cell division (McIntosh et al., 2012; Prosser and Pelletier, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Microtubule architecture in the spindle is governed by the spatiotemporal profile of MT nucleation and the action of molecular motors.
source: It is currently thought that the microtubule (MT) architecture in the spindle is governed by the spatiotemporal profile of MT nucleation and the action of molecular motors (Brugués et al., 2012; Needleman et al., 2010; Oriola et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Spindle microtubules originate from spindle poles, chromosomes, and from the lateral surface of pre-existing spindle microtubules through branching MT nucleation.
source: Spindle MTs originate from spindle poles, chromosomes, and from the lateral surface of pre-existing spindle MTs in a process termed branching MT nucleation (Dinarina et al., 2009; Duncan and Wakefield, 2011; Hayward et al., 2014; Heald et al., 1996; Maresca et al., 2009; Meunier and Vernos, 2016; Petry et al., 2013; Piehl et al., 2004; Prosser and Pelletier, 2017; Tulu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Resolving MT nucleation events in the spindle is challenging due to the high density of microtubules.
source: Because of the high density of MTs resulting from these nucleation pathways, resolving MT nucleation events in the spindle is challenging (Brugués et al., 2012; Burbank et al., 2006; Decker et al., 2018; Kaye et al., 2017; Needleman et al., 2010; Oh et al., 2016; Prosser and Pelletier, 2017; Redemann et al., 2017; Tulu et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research documenting this challenge.

claim: Gamma-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) is the universal nucleator common to all MT nucleation pathways.
source: Common to all MT nucleation pathways is the universal nucleator, gamma-tubulin ring complex (γ-TuRC) (Kollman et al., 2011; Tovey and Conduit, 2018), together with XMAP215/chTOG/Stu2 (Flor-Parra et al., 2018; Gunzelmann et al., 2018; Thawani et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: γ-TuRC is proposed to be positioned and activated at specific sites and times for each nucleation pathway during spindle assembly.
source: γ-TuRC has been proposed to be positioned and turned on at specific sites and times respectively, for each pathway during spindle assembly (Kollman et al., 2011) and a number of factors that perform these functions have been identified (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017; Choi et al., 2010; Cota et al., 2017; Kollman et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2014; Tovey and Conduit, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Branching MT nucleation nucleates new daughter MTs from the surface of pre-existing ones in a narrow range of angles.
source: Branching MT nucleation is an important spindle assembly pathway that nucleates new daughter MTs from the surface of pre-existing ones in a narrow range of angles (Kamasaki et al., 2013; Petry et al., 2013) and, in isolation, creates dense, wedge-shaped networks with uniform polarity (Petry et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Loss of branching components causes reduced MT mass within the spindle body.
source: Loss of branching components causes reduced MT mass within the spindle body (Goshima et al., 2008; Kamasaki et al., 2013; Petry et al., 2011), instability of kinetochore fibers (Bucciarelli et al., 2009; Lawo et al., 2009; Uehara et al., 2009), insufficient tension during chromosome segregation (Uehara et al., 2009), and chromosome misalignment (Goshima et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Branching is the major nucleation pathway in spindles that form without centrosomes.
source: Most importantly, branching is the major nucleation pathway in spindles that form either without centrosomes (Petry et al., 2011) or in larger spindles (e.g. in Xenopus egg extracts), where it generates most of the MT mass (Decker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Augmin binds to the nucleator γ-TuRC and recruits it to existing MTs.
source: The multisubunit complex augmin has been characterized as a targeting factor that binds to the nucleator γ-TuRC and recruits it to existing MTs in several model systems (Kamasaki et al., 2013; Nakaoka et al., 2012; Petry et al., 2011; Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2016; Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: TPX2 is necessary for branching MT nucleation.
source: The protein TPX2 is necessary for branching MT nucleation (Petry et al., 2013) and was recently proposed to activate γ-TuRC (Alfaro-Aco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Branching events occur primarily near the minus-ends of pre-existing MTs and are excluded from the vicinity of plus-ends.
source: Upon careful analysis, we consistently observed that branching events occurred primarily near the minus-ends of pre-existing MTs and were excluded from the vicinity of plus-ends (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Microtubules branch at a shallow angle with 0° median angle and a standard deviation of 9°.
source: We find that MTs branch at a shallow angle with 0° median angle and a standard deviation (s.d.) of 9°.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B (n=339 measurements from 19 branched networks).

claim: The growth speed of MT plus-ends during growth was 8.3 ± 2.5 μm min−1.
source: The speed of plus-ends during growth was 8.3 ± 2.5 μm min−1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), similar to previous reports (Tirnauer et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The net plus-end speed over the entire MT trajectory was vpe = 5.3 ± 1.4 μm min−1.
source: The net plus-end speed over the entire MT trajectory, including growth, catastrophe, and pause phases, was vpe = 5.3 ± 1.4 μm min−1 (n = 115 MT tracks).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from 115 MT tracks.

claim: The number of MTs in the network increased exponentially over time with an effective autocatalytic nucleation rate of 0.54 ± 0.06 min−1.
source: The number of MTs in the network, counted via the number of EB1 comets where each EB1 comet marks a single MT, increased exponentially over time with an effective autocatalytic nucleation rate of 0.54 ± 0.06 min−1 (n = 11 branched networks, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from 11 branched networks shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: MT lengths were exponentially distributed in branched networks.
source: MT lengths were exponentially distributed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–E) with an average length that approached a steady value over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D, red curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Branched MT networks are in a bounded growth regime.
source: Thus, branched MT networks are in a bounded growth regime, in agreement with previous measurements made in the spindle (Dogterom and Leibler, 1993; Ishihara et al., 2016; Verde et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The single-step model does not display an exclusion zone near the plus-end or a non-dimensional bias in branching location.
source: The single-step model does not display an exclusion zone near the plus-end (Figure 2A, red curve) or a non-dimensional bias (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The sequential model recapitulates the bias in branch location from the older lattice near the minus-end and the resulting exclusion of the plus-ends.
source: In contrast, the sequential model recapitulates the bias in branch location from the older lattice near the minus-end and the resulting exclusion of the plus-ends (Figure 2A–B, green curves), as more nucleation sites deposit on the older lattice while the mother's plus-end continues to grow in the time it takes on average to nucleate a branch from the deposited site.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2A-B and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: Not a single nucleation event was observed in the region 2.1 μm from the plus-end of the mother MT.
source: Surprisingly, not a single nucleation event was observed in the region 2.1 μm from the plus-end of the mother MT (n = 381 measurements), resulting in a dead-zone for branching near the plus-end.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from 381 branched networks.

claim: Most branching events occurred 5–15 μm away from the mother's plus-end.
source: Most branching events occurred 5–15 μm away from the mother's plus-end (Figure 2A, blue curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The minus-end bias persists for every subsequent branching event in a dense network.
source: Our simulations further show that the minus-end bias persists for every subsequent branching event in a dense network, similar to the first nucleation event, and broadly characterizes branched MT networks (compare Figure 2—figure supplement 2D–E with Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Minus-ends are typically located closer to the origin of the network in the sequential model than in the single-step model.
source: By measuring the position of nucleation sites using our simulations, we observed that minus-ends are typically located closer to the origin of the network (defined as the minus-end of the first MT) in the sequential model than in the single-step model (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The total MT mass and plus-ends are closer to the origin in the sequential model compared to the single-step model.
source: Measuring the position of plus-ends as well as the tubulin intensity shows that the total MT mass and plus-ends are also closer to the origin in the sequential model (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The MT plus-ends and tubulin intensity profile in experimental networks are distributed closer to the origin, in agreement with the sequential model.
source: The MT plus-ends and tubulin intensity profile in our experimental networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) are distributed closer to the origin (Figure 2D–E, blue), in striking agreement with the sequential model (Figure 2D–E, green).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 2D-E and comparison with the sequential model.

claim: Branched networks are self-similar in time and maintain their architecture.
source: This suggests that branched networks are self-similar in time and maintain their architecture, which is a key characteristic of fractal structures (Meakin, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C) and experimental observations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D-E), with comparison to fractal structure literature.

claim: Branching was delayed with a decrease in concentration of augmin or TPX2 and accelerated with TPX2 addition.
source: We observed that branching was delayed with a decrease in concentration of augmin or TPX2 and accelerated with TPX2 addition (Video 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Video 5.

claim: TPX2 concentration determines the rate of nucleation in branched networks.
source: Strikingly, TPX2 concentration determines the rate of nucleation in our networks (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Altering the number of TPX2 or augmin molecules in bulk cytoplasm matches equivalent variations in the rate-limiting steps of the sequential model.
source: Altogether, we show that altering the number of TPX2 or augmin molecules in bulk cytoplasm matches equivalent variations in the rate-limiting steps of our sequential model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements (Figure 3B) and comparison with computational modeling.

claim: New branches nucleated from de novo MTs that were formed with TPX2 but without augmin when augmin was subsequently added.
source: To our surprise, new branches (red MTs with EB1-labeled plus-ends in green) nucleated from the de novo MTs (blue) that were formed initially with TPX2 but without augmin (Figure 4A and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments shown in Figure 4A and Video 6.

claim: The first branches appeared as early as 10–30 s within the addition of augmin.
source: Interestingly, the first branches appeared as early as 10–30 s within the addition of augmin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: De novo MTs formed in the presence of augmin but without TPX2, followed by addition of TPX2 without augmin, did not result in branch formation.
source: The reverse sequence, where de novo MTs were formed in the presence of augmin, but without TPX2, followed by a switch to extract with TPX2 but lacking augmin, did not result in branch formation (Figure 4B and Video 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments shown in Figure 4B and Video 6.

claim: Branching MT nucleation is a sequential pathway where TPX2's deposition on de novo MTs precedes the binding of augmin and subsequent branch formation.
source: These results demonstrate that branching MT nucleation is a sequential pathway where TPX2's deposition on the de novo MTs precedes the binding of augmin and subsequent branch formation, while additional soluble TPX2 is not required to generate branches.
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: γ-TuRC is essential together with augmin in the branching pathway after TPX2 binding.
source: This demonstrates that γ-TuRC is essential together with augmin in the branching pathway after TPX2 binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TPX2 associated with individual MTs, including the first de novo MT prior to the formation of the first branched MT.
source: First, we observed that TPX2-GFP associated with individual MTs, including the first de novo MT prior to the formation of the first branched MT (Figure 4D and Video 8), supporting the molecular sequence during branch formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct visualization experiments shown in Figure 4D and Video 8.

claim: The binding of TPX2 to MTs was slow, such that the plus-ends were mostly devoid of TPX2 signal, and a decreasing profile of TPX2 from minus- to plus-ends was observed.
source: The binding of TPX2 to MTs was slow, such that the plus-ends were mostly devoid of TPX2 signal, and a decreasing profile of TPX2 from minus- to plus-ends was observed (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct visualization experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The binding rate of TPX2 to the MT lattice was calculated to be 0.4 ± 0.2 molecules μm−1 s−1.
source: We calculated the binding rate of TPX2 to the MT lattice to be 0.4 ± 0.2 molecules μm−1 s−1 (n = 32 traces).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements from 32 traces shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TPX2's measured binding rate is too slow to saturate the newly formed MT lattice.
source: Notably, TPX2's measured binding rate is too slow to saturate the newly formed MT lattice, which presents approximately 250 inter-protofilament dimer sites per micron per second (Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of measured TPX2 binding rate with the number of available binding sites on the MT lattice, with citation to previous research.

claim: The slow binding kinetics of TPX2 results in its localization on the older lattice regions near the MT minus-ends.
source: Hence, the slow binding kinetics of TPX2 results in its localization on the older lattice regions near the MT minus-ends, corresponding to its role in marking the nucleation sites in our sequential kinetic model.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of TPX2 binding rate and mechanistic reasoning.

claim: Augmin and γ-TuRC were not present initially on individual MTs but appear later as more MTs nucleate in the branched networks.
source: Direct visualization of GFP-tagged recombinant augmin or fluorescent γ-TuRC antibody during branched network formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–E) showed that augmin and γ-TuRC were not present initially on individual MTs but appear later as more MTs nucleate in the branched networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by direct visualization experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: Nucleation in branched networks is spatially biased towards the older lattice regions near the MT minus-ends.
source: By combining precise experimental perturbations with image analysis tools, mathematical modeling, and detailed measurements, we show that nucleation in branched networks is spatially biased towards the older lattice regions near the MT minus-ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements (Figure 2A-B) and computational modeling.

claim: Branching MT nucleation is a sequential process involving deposition of nucleation sites by TPX2 and delayed branching by the augmin/γ-TuRC complex.
source: We demonstrate that branching MT nucleation is a sequential process involving deposition of nucleation sites by TPX2 and delayed branching by the augmin/γ-TuRC complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments (Figure 4A-C) and direct visualization of TPX2 binding (Figure 4D-E).

claim: Mechanisms involving only the direct localization of nucleators augmin/γ-TuRC to MTs do not result in branch formation.
source: In particular, mechanisms involving either only the direct localization of nucleators augmin/γ-TuRC to MTs, or the localization followed by the rate-limiting activation of augmin/γ-TuRC (Kollman et al., 2011) do not result in branch formation (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments shown in Figure 4A-B and comparison with previous models.

claim: TPX2's localization on individual MTs is necessary before augmin/γ-TuRC to nucleate a branch.
source: Instead, TPX2's localization on individual MTs is necessary before augmin/γ-TuRC to nucleate a branch.
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Branching MT nucleation is not a result of independent binding of TPX2 and augmin to the MT lattice.
source: Second, we show that branching MT nucleation is not a result of independent binding of TPX2 and augmin to the MT lattice, an activity that has been shown for both proteins in vitro (Brunet et al., 2004; Hsia et al., 2014; Roostalu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments (Figure 4A-B) and comparison with previous in vitro studies.

claim: The nucleator γ-TuRC cannot be recruited by TPX2 independently, but requires augmin.
source: Third, we find that the nucleator γ-TuRC cannot be recruited by TPX2 independently, but requires augmin (Figure 4C), which could not be ruled out based on previous work.
evidence: This claim is supported by solution exchange experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The length distribution of MTs in branched networks displays a bounded growth regime, as reported for centrosomes in mitosis.
source: The length distribution of MTs in branched networks displays a bounded growth regime, as reported for centrosomes in mitosis (Verde et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D-E) and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The net branching nucleation rate directly measured (0.5 min−1) agrees with previous estimates from monopolar spindles (3 min−1) and RanGTP asters (1.2 min−1).
source: The net branching nucleation rate we directly measured (0.5 min−1) agrees with previous estimates from monopolar spindles (3 min−1; Decker et al., 2018) and RanGTP asters (1.2 min−1; Clausen and Ribbeck, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and comparison with previous literature.

claim: The preferential nucleation from older MT lattice regions could allow for precise control over where branching occurs in the spindle.
source: Third, and most importantly, the preferential nucleation from older MT lattice regions could allow for precise control over where branching occurs in the spindle.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental findings and their implications for spindle organization.

claim: TPX2, which is released in the vicinity of chromosomes, accumulates on the older MT lattice regions near chromosomes.
source: We propose that TPX2, which is released in the vicinity of chromosomes (Kalab et al., 2002; Oh et al., 2016), accumulates on the older MT lattice regions near chromosomes such as on MTs captured and stabilized by the kinetochores (Cimini et al., 2003; DeLuca et al., 2011; Lampson et al., 2004; Umbreit et al., 2012) and older lattice regions such as minus-ends near the spindle center.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and previous literature about TPX2 localization.

claim: Branching MT nucleation by augmin/γ-TuRC from deposited TPX2 sites will selectively amplify older MTs generating dense kinetochore fibers near chromosomes.
source: Branching MT nucleation by augmin/γ-TuRC from deposited TPX2 sites will selectively amplify older MTs generating dense kinetochore fibers near chromosomes.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: The endogenous concentration of TPX2 was estimated as 20–30 nM in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: The endogenous concentration was estimated as 20–30 nM in Xenopus egg extracts.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence western blot measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Partial depletion of TPX2 resulted in 20% of endogenous concentration remaining.
source: For 80% depletion of endogenous TPX2, 14 µg of purified anti-TPX2 antibody (0.14 mg/ml purified stock) was coupled with 100 µl Dynabeads overnight and was incubated with 100 µl egg extract for 20 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental protocol and western blot analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Partial depletion of augmin resulted in 20% HAUS8, 36% HAUS6, 54% HAUS1, and 70% γ-TuRC and GCP4 remaining compared to control.
source: Protein levels in augmin depletion compared to control depletion: HAUS8 (20%), HAUS6 (36%), HAUS1 (54%), γ-tubulin and GCP4 (70% each).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative fluorescence western blot measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The distance of the first branching site from the mother MT's minus- or plus-end increased with decreasing TPX2 or augmin to 20% endogenous concentration.
source: The distance of the first branching site from the mother MT's minus- or plus-end increased with decreasing TPX2 or augmin to 20% endogenous concentration (red and yellow curves, Figure 3B, top and middle panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Increasing the concentration of TPX2 to 9.6-fold decreases the distance between nucleation site and mother MT's minus- or plus-end.
source: Similarly, increasing the concentration of TPX2 to 9.6-fold decreases the distance between nucleation site and mother MT's minus- or plus-end, which quantitatively compares with equivalent increase in kbind or kbranch (green curve, Figure 3B, top and middle panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The non-dimensional spatial bias remains unaltered upon varying the rate constants by 5–10 fold in the sequential model.
source: Finally, our model predicts that the non-dimensional spatial bias remains unaltered upon varying the rate constants by 5–10 fold, which was reproduced in experimental profiles upon equivalent change in concentration of TPX2 or augmin (Figure 3B, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling predictions and experimental measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Augmin and γ-TuRC have been shown to bind directly at low concentrations.
source: Augmin and γ-TuRC have been shown to bind directly at low concentrations (Song et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Rare branches were observed at later time points in γ-TuRC depletion experiments due to residual γ-TuRC molecules after immunodepletion.
source: We note that rare branches were observed at later time points (Figure 4C, rightmost panel) due to residual γ-TuRC molecules after immunodepletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Localization of augmin to MTs in the cytoplasm is mediated by other proteins, potentially by TPX2.
source: Based on our results (Figure 4A–B), we speculate that localization of augmin to MTs in the cytoplasm is mediated by other proteins, as suggested recently for human augmin (Luo et al., 2019), and potentially by TPX2.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on experimental results and comparison with recent literature.

claim: The minor differences between experimental nucleation profiles and the sequential model may indicate the involvement of undiscovered effectors, or time-dependent regulation of known effectors.
source: Finally, we note that our work does not rule out the participation of other, yet unknown effectors in branching MT nucleation. The minor differences between our experimental nucleation profiles and the sequential model (Figure 2) may indicate the involvement of undiscovered effectors, or time-dependent regulation of known effectors.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison of experimental and modeling results.
